review:
[h1][Introduction][/h1]
I would like to start this review with saying that I’m usually not really into puzzle games, let alone games with actual puzzle pieces, the majority of those are just boring to me. But this one seems to be special, it just hit me when I saw the trailer and screenshots; I guess the aesthetic and audio just spoke to me.

As in all my reviews, these are my own opinions and experiences, please check out other reviews too!

[h1][Negatives/Suggestions][/h1]
Puzzle pieces are slightly larger when you pick them up, this can result in frustration and confusion when you just can’t find the right spots. Some keys or arrows would’ve been nice to turn the piece tray without the needing to grab it. Spinning it happen often accidentally when you just want to grab a piece. 

Having to pick up the pieces in order to see the colors can be a bit tiresome if you’re looking for distinct colors, an option to at least slightly see the color would be cool. The game is simply too short and can be finished in around 3-4 hours which was a bit disappointing; I was hoping for more. New puzzles as DLC or a sequel would be great. An option to show solved puzzles in fullscreen without any UI elements would’ve been a nice add to create pretty screenshots or even wallpapers.

[h1][Gameplay][/h1]
Just what you would expect from a jigsaw puzzle game. Picking up the puzzle pieces to drop them in the right spot to complete the whole picture. There is no time or move limit so this adds to the relaxing atmosphere of the game. What makes it different is that no piece is the same, each one has a different shape and size and the overall puzzle shape varies widely as well.

While most of the game is rather easy, some specific puzzles can be quite challenging; one of them took me 20 minutes to beat it. There are 25 unique puzzles in 25 different countries related to events that happened in said countries. It was fun to guess the picture while getting closer to the reveal.

[h1][Graphics/Art][/h1]
This right here is a unique mix of majestically fitting menus mixed together with beautiful stained glass artwork. The whole game is just so mysterious and colorful that it tends to mesmerize you pretty much the whole time. Artworks are based on the specific countries history and pretty much all of them are just a pleasure to look at.

[h1][Music][/h1]
A soundtrack fitting the mysterious nature of the game is also included and helps greatly with creating a relaxing atmosphere. Each section of earth has a proper song with instruments unique to that zone, doing a great job of conveying the part of earth you are currently in.

[url=http://www.nikcomposer.com/]Checkout the composers website for a preview![/url] 

[h1][Conclusion][/h1]
With 3-4 hours playtime, the price is justified in my opinion and this is certainly a pleasure for people who enjoy those kind of games with the added bonus of this also being very relaxing and fun. I recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the game just based on the screenshots and people who are interested in jigsaw puzzle games.

For now, it’s the the best jigsaw puzzle game I’ve ever seen. The authentic and artistic combination of instrumental music and stained glass art is just too lovely!

A good game that could have been great. As much as I love the concept behind the game - as much as I wanted to love the game itself - there are too many technical problems with its execution to make it enjoyable. 

Glass Masquerade is essentially a jigsaw puzzle game, where pieces can be any shape and any size:
- You can only see the cutout shape of each piece before you drag it on the board. The actual colours and patterns are hidden.
- Sizes of individual pieces are not to scale before you drag it on the board. This means that two pieces which appear to be similarly sized can be, and oftentimes are, actually vastly different in size. 
- The pieces are arranged in two concentric wheels around the board. It is extremely easy to pick up the wrong piece (e.g. from one wheel instead of the other wheel). It also means you can't see all the available pieces until you place about 50% of them onto the board. 
- Even when you place the correct piece in the correct place, it sometimes takes up to three tries before the piece will lock in place. This is extremely unhelpful when you aren't 100% certain that you have the right piece, and you waste entire minutes trying to figure out what other piece could go in that position... until you realize it was just the game not registering.

All these flaws put together make the game just a painful experience of trial-and-error. If you can't see what's on each piece, or know exactly how large each piece is, or see all the available pieces simultaneously, or even be sure when you place the piece correctly... How can you jigsaw? 

The interface is fine, the puzzles themselves are beautiful, the soundtrack is relaxing.  But if the crux of the game is practically unplayable, none of that matters.

Judging by the plethora of positive reviews (which originally convinced me to buy the game for myself), I am in the minority with my complaints. I don't have anything against the game, I don't think it is a bad game; but I do know that there will be many people out there who, like me, will not have a good time playing it.

Very beautiful. Very relaxing gameplay. I encountered no bugs and I love the soundtrack! 
I also like that you touch upon many national myths and legends in the pictures you put together. 

The only thing that annoys me is the fact you get no world overview, at least I found no way to zoom out of the closer view. And half of the screen (when you are scrolling along the world map to chose your next destination) is taken up by the last jigsaw you solved, even after re-entering the game. So later on it gets a bit tedious to find the jigsaws you have yet to solve. But that's just menu navigation - and even though I'm itching for this overview because I think it would be very satisfying to see my progress, I try to forget that during the actual gameplay. 
There is also a different view of your progress right at the start of the game (national flags of the countries you already visited), so I guess that will have to do...

[h1] 8/10 [/h1]

As a very common casual puzzle game, Glass Masquerade does not expand too much in terms of gameplay. Its gameplay and design are very simple, no matter what type of player can quickly get the hang of it. The most attractive thing about this game is undoubtedly its dazzling and shocking glass art.

The game brings together the art and cultural styles of various countries, through the way of puzzles, players can intuitively enjoy a visual feast of the International Times Exhibition. The satisfaction that can be brought to the player when all the puzzles are finally completed is unparalleled.

Glass Masquerade is perfect for players who are attracted by the artistic style of this work, are interested in jigsaw puzzles, and looking for a game to kill the time. However, the gameplay is actually not very good, except for the puzzles, there is no other content in the game, and overall its artistry is much greater than its gameplay. Its biggest advantage is that any player can enjoy its fun fully.

Short Version:

Pros
+ Beautiful visuals
+ Soothing soundtrack
+ Relaxing

Cons
- Scrolling through pieces is somewhat clunky

"Long" Version:

[u]Glass Masquerade[/u] is a puzzle game where you must place glass tiles on a board to complete it.

It is a very relaxing game, which does not stress you on any level whatsoever. 

The soundtrack is very subtle and soothing.

The gameplay is very simple; you click on a piece to select it and you can place it on the board, if you click on the correct area, the piece will stay there permanently, bringing you one step closer to completion. In order to scroll through pieces, however, you must click on the tab said pieces are on, and move the mouse up or down. Unfortunately, you'll end up selecting an actual piece instead scrolling more often than not. It is not that big of a deal, however, I got frustrated a few times.

The achievements, for example, are earned for completing the puzzle, instead of being the usual "finish the puzzle under X minutes". You can take your time and simply enjoy it at your own pace, not having to worry about time trials, order of completion, etc.

The game should take you around 4 hours to beat - I recommend completing one or two puzzles at a time, to maximize your enjoyment.

In conclusion, [u]Glass Masquerade[/u] is an amazing game that features great visuals, a very relaxing soundtrack and a very pleasant adventure around the world. I confidently recommend it.

Final Score: 9 out of 10.

It shocks me how positive the reviews of this game is. Yes, the art is gorgeous, yes, the music is exquisite, but outside of that it fails at basic functionality. How are people not commenting on the broken and limited interface?

First off, I was a bit disappointed that every puzzle is a jigsaw puzzle, but okay, my mistake for not doing more research. For some reason they shy away from the word 'jigsaw' in the description. Combining hidden glass pieces at an interactive electronic show sounds so much better and not at all pretentious, but I digress. It's a jisaw puzzle game that fails at basic jigsaw mechanics.

You would think the number one priority of a jigsaw is that the pieces look like they can fit together, right? Except the outline of the puzzle pieces is so thick that most of the time your pieces will look much too big to fit into the puzzle. Way too often I was baffled when a piece actually snapped into place. The nature of the art and how it's sectioned off also makes it very difficult to use the picture as a guide for where pieces ought to go; the highly stylized art means that most of the shapes and colours kinda blend together until you have completed the picture. So you can't trust the piece outlines, and you can't trust the picture.

What frustrated me the most (to the point where I decided to leave a review) was how the interface is working against you. The pieces you have yet to put in place are arranged on two wheels surrounding the puzzle, and half of each is hidden from sight until you use up a good chunk of your pieces. You rotate the wheels by clicking and dragging, except they will often not respond at all, or you will grab a puzzle piece on accident. I genuinely got stuck at one point because the wheel refused to turn, and I thought I had no more pieces left outside of the ones in view. They give you a few freebie pieces at the beginning of each puzzle, so they obviously must have figured out that something was unintuitive and difficult here.

Sure, the price point is pretty fair for what you are getting. I'm happy to pay this much for the art and music by themselves, and the OST of the game is provided for free when you buy it. So just put the soundtrack on, find yourself a jigsaw with pieces that actually fit together, maybe you even have a table to spread the pieces out on for a quick and easy overview, and then you can just google some stained glass art and have a better experience.

Seems like the most important thing to know when considering this game is that it's NOT a conventional jigsaw puzzle. If you're into those and go in expecting to do your usual thing, you'll be disappointed... Or maybe pleasantly surprised, if you're open to something different. 

Instead of being presented with all the puzzle pieces to sort as you please and a goal image for orientation, you just semi-blindly pick up piece after piece, see if you can find its place this time, and figure things out as you go. Trying to guess what the image is and sometimes only realizing when placing the last piece was part of the fun for me. 

The special aesthetics are obviously a major selling point for this game. Cool transitions into and out of the menus and levels almost make it feel like you're playing around with some kind of Steampunk device. I liked scrolling around the map to plan my "journey" and choose the next country. Having some geography knowledge probably helps with orientation, otherwise there's some educational value (: 
The enchanting music and the glassy sound effects when placing a puzzle piece complete the experience. 

It's not very nice that you can't finish everything on the map without buying all the DLCs, but I guess it was easiest to implement it that way. Also understandable that they want to advertise the DLCs, especially considering the low prices for a decently long high-quality experience. 
The achievements can all be... achieved? without buying DLCs. 

I found it a bit too easy to accidentally move the disks instead of the puzzle pieces, but it wasn't more than a minor annoyance for me. It works fine if you drag them towards the center of the puzzle. Other people have struggled with accidentally moving puzzle pieces instead of the disk, but 1. you can just figure out the visible pieces first, 2. you can rotate the disks using your scroll wheel to avoid "misunderstandings". 

Other than that? I often find games with "overwhelmingly positive" reviews overhyped, but this one deserves them imo.

[b][i]Glass Masquerade[/i][/b] is a pure puzzle game where the player must put together stained glass murals inside of clocks from the pieces given to them at the start.  There are a total of [b]25[/b] handcrafted puzzles for you to enjoy, with an additional [b]25[/b] puzzles available to you through the various DLCs for the game, for a total of [b]50[/b] handcrafted puzzles.

The premise of the game is simple: rebuild the stained glass murals that are found inside of clocks from the pieces given to you at the start of the puzzle.  Each puzzle piece fits together like a jigsaw puzzle piece, and each piece can only go in one specific location in the puzzle.  There is no rotation of the pieces in this game, so those of you that don't like having to rotate their puzzle pieces to finish the puzzle can rejoice about this fact!  

Puzzle sizes range from around 30 pieces to 60 pieces in the base game, and up to 71 pieces in one particular DLC puzzle, so they aren't too terribly taxing on the mind (until you get to the larger puzzles with 60+ pieces).  If you are someone that enjoys easier puzzles, then this is the game for you!

Overall, the game mechanics are solid, however, I ran into a few issues while playing the game (one of which I believe is caused by my mouse):

1. The area where you can place a puzzle piece and have it count as "correct" and snap into place is very small, making for some really frustrating times trying to place it [i]just[/i] right to make it stick in the puzzle.
2. Sometimes when I clicked a puzzle piece, it was immediately placed back down without me releasing the mouse button or doing anything else with the mouse.  Sometimes, this happened 5-6 times in a row.  Extremely frustrating (I think this might be caused by my mouse, but if you had this same problem without any issues from your mouse, please let me know in the comments!)
3. Sometimes, on the puzzle piece selection wheel, one piece moves and combines with another piece (basically lays on top of the other piece), making it hard to select the piece underneath it.

Even given these facts, I still think that the game mechanics are extremely solid and are nearly perfect in all aspects.

The music composed for this game fits it like a glove, but over time, can become somewhat grating to listen to while trying to solve the puzzles.  That being said, they are still great pieces to listen to.  I think, though, if you wanted to make it less grating over time, making this game have more than 6 pieces of music would help.

The main problem I have with this game is that it is too short.  My rule of thumb when buying a game is a 2:1 return on my money in terms of # of hours gotten from a game to the cost of the game.  So, for this game, I was expecting around 10 hours, but only got ~8.5 hours of play, and given the fact the most of the puzzles in the game are fairly easy, this game is very easy to complete in a single gameplay session.  While I do understand that this game is meant to be this way, I still was looking for a little bit more out of my money.

Here's the list of pros, neutrals and cons as explained above:

Pros:

+ Solid gameplay mechanics.
+ Very original and beautiful puzzle compositions!
+ Enjoyable music (for a while)

Neutral:

Most puzzles are on the somewhat easy side.
Music gets grating after listening to it for >1 hour or so.
A few quirks encountered while solving puzzles, such as difficulty grabbing pieces and difficulty finding the right spot for them in the puzzle.

Cons:
- Piece combination bug is frustrating.

Overall, this is a great experience for puzzle purists and I highly recommend it and all DLCs at full price!

Only con: not very long, it should last you around 2-3 hours

Really recommended: relaxing, fun and very good looking!

This game is a classic jigsaw puzzle game. I would certainly recommend it, but at a discount. Here is the practical breakdown:

CONS:
1. The game is too easy and short. No piece rotation and odd boarder shapes made it not challenging
2. There are no difficulty settings, so you can't make the puzzles harder by having it broken into more pieces
3. Pieces do not exactly match the openings they fit in. If it kinda looks like it fits, try it.
4. The pieces are in rings that spin. This is more annoying then helpful and sometime the wheels spin on one side and not the other to reveal other pieces you did not know were hiding.

PROS:
1. Absolutely beautiful. I would actually love to have a time piece that looked like some of these.
2. The shapes of the pieces were also interesting making the game more engaging.
3. The music was relaxing and changed from location to location to prevent it from being too repetitive
4. Puzzles were stylistic representations of something having to do with the country they are for as did some of the music

***RECOMENDATION***
1. In the settings for the game, make sure you deselect the starting clues. The game was already too easy. I cannot imagine how much faster it would have been with help.

All in all, I really enjoyed the experience of piecing these beautiful artistic works together. If you are in the mood for something quick and visual, this is it.

Recommended.

Story...

There's not much of a story for a pure puzzle game, but I didn't expect anything more. The idea is very simple; explore the world via puzzles. That's it, and it's fine the way it is.

Gameplay...

It was both challenging and rewarding. There were varying difficulties, from three to five - and five being the most challenging. The puzzles had different shapes, which made some of them quite difficult. They certainly were different from normal rectangle ones, for instance. 

There was also this interesting trick. Depending what route you went, you could come across puzzles with the difficulty rate being five. After finishing it and unlocking the next, that puzzle's difficulty could be four. I actually ended enjoying that, since I could test my skill and then relax a bit more with a more easy puzzle.

Art...

The art was really pleasant to look at. As I don't know much about stained glass art, I'm not sure if they are "real" or just made for the game. Either way, they were pretty and I even learned some history from them.

Music...

At first, it annoyed me. The music itself didn't sound bad, but my focus drifted because of it, especially if the puzzle was hard. After I finished the last five puzzles, the music didn't bother me at all.

Conclusion...

It's a nice, short game that can offer either challenge or relaxation. There's no time limits, so there's no need to rush to get that one achievement. You might learn new things from playing the game. However, I think the price is just a bit too high for a game that will take two to three hours to finish. Unless you buy it on sale.

This game is just gorgeous. Incredibly aesthetically pleasing and relaxing. When I first bought the game, I intended to savour it over quite a while but I couldn't resist. Played it in two sessions, only stopping the first time because it was getting late and it ended up appearing in my dreams that night. 

Pros: 
- Art. The main feature. The stained glass. The guilded edges of the pieces. The whole colour palette, I could gush about the art forever. It's beautiful to me in a wtf-how-can-something-be-so-beautiful kind of way. 
- Music. When you're playing a game for a long period of time, music is very important. It can be incredibly annoying if it's a short track with a clear beginning and end that just loops continuously. I've played this game for hours straight and the music was still very pleasant to my ears. Suits the game incredibly well.
- Unique puzzle pieces. After having completed a whole lot of puzzles with traditional shapes, this is really refereshing. No two pieces are the same shape. 
- No need to rotate pieces. The pieces on the sides aren't in the same position they will be on the board but when you pick up a piece, it auto-rotates for you. 
- Sounds. A bit hard to describe but something as simple as the sounds of the cursor mousing over certain areas that become highlighted, clicking on clickable things, and picking up and setting down puzzle pieces are satisfyingly pleasant. 
- The option to have hint fragments at the start. It can be pretty difficult trying to solve the puzzle blind and a few hint edge pieces are good to start you off. 
- Small halo of light around the pieces. This helps primarily when you're holding a piece and trying to see where it might go on the clock. It's helpful but not really a solution.  
- The price for the content. If you manage to get this while it's on sale like it is now, it's a real bargain. 

Possible cons and suggestions for improvement: 
- Once you pick up a piece, if you don't put it in the correct place, it'll go back to the sidelines. This means that you can't connect pieces together or leave pieces on the clock. I personally don't have any issue with this because the pieces are all spaced out nicely on the sides so there's no chance of a piece getting lost in the mosaic.
- When there are dark puzzle pieces or even dark parts of puzzle pieces, it can be difficult to see where they go since they blend into the dark background. I understand it's a part of the whole theme and colour palette of the game but it would be nice for the ability to change the background colour of the clocks. Or it could be something like 'turning on the light' where the background becomes illuminated like a jack o' lantern. 
- There no picture of the completed puzzle until you've completed it at least once and even then, it can only be seen from the map. Also not a con for me because the irregular pieces mean it's easier to know where each piece goes and there's the pleasant feeling of mystery around what the image will be as it comes together.
- The wheel or whatever the mechanism is called on the sides of the clock where the pieces lie. It can be a bit of a pain not being able to see all the pieces at once and sometimes I click on it with the intention of dragging to move the wheel but end up picking up a piece, even though I didn't click on a piece. Doesn't happen too often but it's a thing. 

Highly recommended if you like jigsaw puzzles and the art. Excited for the sequel.

I’ve played all four Glass Masquerade games, and Glass Masquerade 1 is still my favourite. The art is really beautiful. Each puzzle looks like stained glass that is glowing with soft light. The designs are inspired by different countries, and each one feels like a small piece of culture shown through art. The gameplay is very calm and relaxing. You match glass pieces by shape and color. Because the pictures are so detailed, you don’t just rely on patterns. Instead, you also think about how the shapes fit together. The pieces are shown in clean rotating rings, so it never feels too messy or overwhelming. The game is also quite short. There are only 25 puzzles, and most of them can be finished quickly in a few minutes. After finishing, there is not much reason to replay it. Overall, Glass Masquerade 1 is a calm and beautiful puzzle game that feels like interactive stained glass art.

Casual visual search puzzles, generally well-built, and a decent chunk of gameplay. Great for the right audience, but I would offer 2 notes:

[b][1] It's not at all like a jigsaw puzzle, despite appearances.[/b] 
When solving a physical jigsaw puzzle you have (a) the "goal" image of the completed puzzle in front of you, and (b) every un-placed piece laid out on the table, face up, and (c) (for most folks/cases) a very limited number of puzzle-piece shapes that you need to fit together. [i]Glass Masquerade[/i] is roughly the inverse. [i]Contra[/i] (a), you don't know what the final image is supposed to be. [i]Contra[/i] (b), all un-placed pieces are face-down (and in a random orientation) except the 1 you click on to select and flip over and try placing. [i]Contra[/i] (c), nearly every puzzle piece is a different shape.

Now, one of my core strategies for solving jigsaw puzzles  is roughly this: see a gap for an unplaced piece, look to the goal image to see what the missing piece should look like, scan the unplaced pieces on the table looking for a match by the colors/image-fragments onit, mentally rotating as needed. And none of that is even an option in [i]Glass Masquerade[/i]. So, if you solve jigsaw puzzled like I do, note that this ain't that. 

[b][2] Unplaced pieces sometimes appear mis-scaled before you place them.[/b]
I played on Steam Deck handheld, so this may have been exacerbated by my smallish screen. But any un-placed piece appears to have a gold outline around its outer edges. Very often, many segments of the outline disappear after the piece is placed. And yet, some remain, because they represent the metal fillings between the panes of stained glass in the puzzle you're building. This means that  pieces very often "look slightly too big" to fit into their correct place. 

This means that trying to match a piece to its correct position is never really a visual search that will generate a 100% match. So you need to look for "fuzzy" matches.

These 2 caveats are enough that I personally left the game wishing I had just done a jigsaw puzzle instead. It was fine, but I doubt I will play any more in the series.

Glass Masquerade is a game for people that enjoy puzzles. It's not for people that find puzzles tedious, nor is it for those that find joy in tediously assembling a hundred identical pieces and feel that starting from the edge and corner pieces is "cheap". It's simply a fun way to pass the time, whether in 10-20 minute bursts when you're bored, or in one continuous cozy afternoon.

The stained glass aesthetic not only allows for unique shape pieces, but also it's simply beautiful to look at. The soundtrack is incredibly relaxing (and can be downloaded separately, for no additional cost). And considering the amount of content even BEFORE DLCs (none of which NEED to be bought to 100% Achievements, thanks to the built-in Demo levels), the price (even outside of sales) feels quite fair to me.

In the end, I certainly recommend game, as these puzzles succeeded in giving me peace.

What can I say about this game? It's a slick and stylish jigsaw puzzle? True, but not very inspiring. It's much better than that though, which is down to the presentation, easy-to-use UI, quality (and the beautiful "stained glass" theme) of the artwork, relaxing music and overall polish. It took me a few hours spread over quite a few nights, generally doing one puzzle a night, but you could power through it in a couple of hours if you were so inclined. The game seems to demand a more measured approach though, and it's the ideal thing to relax with at the end of the day. There's a timer if you want to beat your fastest score, but I'm not sure how replayable this is really.

Criticisms? It would be nice to zoom out of the map to navigate more easily, and it would be great if the buttons on the menu were live at all times, instead of having to wait for the slow, sliding animation to complete.

Delightful puzzle game with absolutely gorgeous artwork and varying levels of difficulty. DLC's add to the map and keep your previously solved puzzles intact.

Glass Masquerade is not about action, adventure, or strategy. It is strictly about solving jigsaw puzzles. It reminds of the days when I had to physically fit jigsaw pieces into the right places in the puzzle before the digital age. It is a casual game with relaxing music that puzzle enthusiasts would love to play.

This indie game features 25 jigsaw puzzles, each representing a country. They are countries across different continents of the world. When you choose a country, you are presented with a clock in which you pick up stained-glass shards on the sides. The game gives you a head start by providing you with highlighted glass shards that you pick up and place on the sides. Then you need to use your spatial abilities to determine which shards go where. Clocks are of various shapes and sizes. They are not complicated for the most part, as some countries are more challenging than others. You can scroll with your mouse wheel to find as many shards as possible to fit them in the correct places.

At the end of solving the puzzle you will see a title of the puzzle and it tends to reflect a country’s tradition such as famous landmarks, mythical people/spirits, animals, and special days of the year. The replay value feels a bit limited after inspecting 25 countries, but the DLCs add more puzzles/countries to solve. From the screenshots and strong reviews, I expected to like this game. My encounters with traditional tabletop jigsaw puzzles are typically limited to annually assembling one with my family throughout the Christmas holidays, but I enjoy that experience when it comes around: the process of methodically laying out pieces by shape and colour group, of laying out edge pieces, then progressively filling in the interior as patterns and groups become visible. I was attracted to the idea of a game which explored that, and liked the historical and geographical twist of associating each puzzle with a country and blending in the visual motifs of that region.

This game has none of that. Instead, the unpopulated piece outlines are only that: outlines. You can only see the full detail of a piece while “holding” it, or after it's been placed. And you can't rotate pieces while they're in the tray: no, the outlines are displayed at some arbitrary rotation, and the pieces are automatically rotated to the correct orientation for you when you pick them up. Pieces can't be temporarily placed on the puzzle surface: they must live in the tray or be placed correctly. Moreover, pieces aren't displayed to scale in the tray, so you have to remember which were large and which were small. To make matters worse, puzzle piece overlap slightly when placed, so all of the outlines are larger than the space the piece will fit into; additionally, the enlarged outlines obscure fine details around piece edges and can make it very difficult to discern the appropriate neighbours for a piece until all of them are in place. This leads to a tedious trial-and-error routine of picking up each available piece in succession, reaquainting yourself with its size, and trying to see if there's anywhere it obviously fits. If so, drop it there and see if it snaps into place; if not, move on to the next piece.

Puzzle difficulties are bizarre and confusing. Each puzzle is rated on a five-star difficulty scale with one star presumably being the least difficult, and five the most. I say “presumably” because I've yet to see a one-star-rated puzzle: the very first puzzle you're given to play is rated three stars, and having explored all my way through the Americas, Europe, Africa, and all the way into China, I've seen only a handful of puzzles rated with two stars. Most are four or five. And even if the scale were reduced to four stars, it still wouldn't make any sense: actual difficulty doesn't seem to be in any way reflected by the assigned celestial count. By way of example, both Ireland and Portugal are rated as being the highest difficult, while I completed the first in an agonizing 13:29, and the later in a blistering 3:53. (For reference, most four-star puzzles seem to take me around four of your Earth minutes.) I think the difficulty measure is based solely on piece count: while both of those puzzles had a high number of pieces, Ireland's puzzle was chock full of intricate details, whereas Portugal's was practically symmetrical.

On the upshot, puzzles look great. The artwork is highly consistent, and the UI complements the puzzles well. Then again, for a game which seems to pride itself on its art, the music is bland and repetitive. It sounds like someone blended a CD of elevator muzak with the soundtrack from a Nancy Drew game. It is technically very high-fidelity, but musically grating. The limited number of tracks broadly incorporate musical themes and stereotypes from different geographic areas, which is conceptually a nice touch, but only helps to emphasize the monotony when multiple successive puzzles share the same backing track.

There isn't much to write home about on a technical level, good or bad. The game is a little quirky in that the main puzzle interface treats both the left and right mouse buttons identically (and maybe the menus do too; I didn't try). You can either click and drag puzzle pieces into place, or click to pick them up, and click again to drop them; while it's nice of the game to be accommodating like that, I found that this got in the way a lot when attempting to spin the trays and I'd end up accidentally picking up a piece instead. This seemed to happen with the left tray in particular, but that might just be a quirk of how I move my mouse. Additionally, over the span of two hours of gameplay, I did run into three instances where I picked up a piece but couldn't put it back down again no matter how many times I clicked. In all three cases, Alt+Tabbing out of the game then back in again fixed it. I'll chalk that up to a case of the Unities.

Overall, I'm not sure who the target audience is for this game, but it's not me. I found it frustrating, unrewarding, and largely unenjoyable. While I did have some fun learning how I think the game wants to be played, that's ultimately not how I want to play the game, so it's not for me. Maybe it'll be for you – it seems to work for lots of other people.

Glass Masquerade tints its jigsaw puzzling stained glass windows with plenty of polish, ensuring its crystallised simplicity has an adequate shine to the fragmented shards.

WHAT I LIKED:
+ Around the world in three hours. Glass Masquerade is a jigsaw puzzle game, lending its connecting of fragments to the artistic form of stained glass. The player is tasked in completing each of the colourful puzzles highlighting cultures from several countries/continents around the globe. From the New York skyline of USA to the bewildering Savannah plains of Africa. Each of the fully completed stained glass masterpieces truly resemble the characteristics of the country they are representing, and sometimes guessing what the final picture will be is half the fun.
+ Just click and place. Replicating jigsaw puzzles to the medium of video gaming can often be a monotonous task. Supply thousands upon thousands of images from across the web and generate a flurry of pieces to put back together, and you have yourself a game. Glass Masquerade differentiates itself by providing its own unique range of majestic art work and, most importantly, including an intuitive user interface alongside the stained glass pieces. Silhouetted pieces are presented adjacent to the centre area for which the glass will be constructed, granting the player the ability to rotate through the tens of fragments in order to select the right shard and position it within the puzzle itself. Everything, from the world map menu to the introductory highlighted segments when starting a puzzle, exist with plenty of finesse and ornate design.
+ Not just a circle. A small detail that provided more variety was the mould of each stained glass window. Not every puzzle was a circle. Some were more polygonal than others, offering different fragmented shapes to spice up the puzzle solving. It's a small inclusion, but one that added even more polish.

WHAT I DISLIKED:
- It's bad luck to smash glass. Once each of the puzzles have been re-assembled, that's pretty much it. Glass Masquerade is done. Aside from attempting to beat your time solving each puzzle (no incentive to whatsoever...) there really is not much else on offer. The puzzles have a pre-determined amount of shards and the difficulty for each one cannot be adjusted. Consequently, once you know how to solve one stained glass once, you can do it again and smash the previous record. If you're an expert jigsaw enthusiast, this may be on the easy side...
- "Drag...I said drag dammit!". More often than not, dragging the circular panels to browse through the remaining shards can be a challenge within itself. The game has a hard time differentiating the action of selecting a piece and rotating the display, making for some moments of unnecessary frustration given the relaxing ambience.
- Payment for more puzzles. Various DLCs exist for gaining additional puzzles, which can be tried out through a loving taster puzzle, but they come at a price. Problem is, with respect to the sequel already available, there's really no incentive to purchase these additional puzzles other than to look at how gorgeous the artwork is. A Christmas DLC at a price? Not very festive...

VERDICT:
6/10 stained glass shards

PROS:
+ Simple and doesn't require a time commitment 
+ Very colorful and has some amazing designs on the clock faces
+ Rexlaxing (although puzzles DO record how long it takes for you to complete them, time records are there for you and not meant to make you rush)
+ Low system requirements, so even an underpowered laptop could handle it
+ For this type of puzzle game, the options menu has a lot of features in it
+ Steam Cloud
+ Inexpensive at $4.99 USD (although I purchased it on sale at $3.74 USD)

CONS:
- Almost too simple and straightforward
- Very short (I literally finished the entire game in four hours and I was taking my time) although the store page makes note of this itself, so it shouldn't come as a surprise
- No alternative modes of play
- Not immediately obvious where every puzzle piece goes (as in some clocks have pieces that go on or around the outside of the clock while others don't)
- No reference images to work from, so you're walking into each puzzle blind
- Puzzle pieces aren't always "to scale" so sometimes the piece will fit into a slot that's smaller than it looks

RECOMMEND: Yes. Despite there being some drawbacks to the game, it's a fun, very nice-looking title that's relaxing and easy to learn.

I hate to be this harsh about an indie game that I bought for <$2, but I'm a little shocked about how positive all the reviews are for it, so here goes:

As an undeniably beautiful aesthetic experience, this game is a solid 8.5/10. As an actual jigsaw puzzle game, giving this game a 2/10 seems...generous, honestly. I'd really probably give it a 1.5, because I can at least say that after multiple hours of play, it's never lagged or crashed on me.

First off, when you get past the main loading screen, the world map interface does not allow you to zoom in and out to quickly see at a glance which puzzles you have solved, and which you still have waiting to be "inspected," as they call it. Given that the game actively encourages you to bounce around and solve the puzzles in whatever order you'd like, I found the constant dragging and scrolling to find unsolved puzzles around the map to be moderately annoying before we even get to the actual puzzle interface itself. Not a dealbreaker, if the rest of the game was well-designed, but....

Once we get to the puzzle interface...woof. I can only imagine that the large number of people who have called this game "relaxing" are either not big jigsaw puzzle fans, or not particularly sensitive to visual size & angle differences when trying to solve a puzzle, because the pieces are often literally the wrong size for the holes they're supposed to go in. This makes it the OPPOSITE of relaxing for me, personally, and I've gotten so frustrated with this (incredibly key) aspect that I've quit the game mid-puzzle on multiple occasions now. I know other people have pointed this out, but considering that "solve a jigsaw puzzle" is effectively the ONLY actual gameplay it has going for it, and they CLEARLY bungled that...I'm not sure I can even really call it a proper jigsaw game, quite frankly.

On top of that main issue, the arbitrary-seeming choice to not allow you to actually see the contents of a piece, only its silhouette, unless you are "holding" it—and only allowing you to "hold" a single piece at a time—almost entirely removes your ability to pick pieces out at a glance based on color-matching, which, again, is usually a key aspect of solving jigsaw puzzles. If they did this deliberately to make it harder, I perhaps wouldn't mind it if [i]the silhouettes weren't often misleading because they're the wrong size for the holes they fit in[/i], as discussed above. This takes this problem from "ups the difficulty" to "actively cuts off an easy way to compensate for their other poor design choices." My only guess as to why they'd do this is that keeping all the unplaced pieces as black silhouettes maintains your visual focus on the art in the solved portion of the puzzle at the center, but that feels like a pretty steep game design sacrifice in the name of aesthetics, personally.

Continuing along that theme, I question, too, the baffling design choices for the way you can look at and choose from the pool of available pieces. Going back to the idea that this is an [i]aesthetically[/i] beautiful game, I understand on a visual level why they'd place the pieces in concentric rings going out from the puzzle at the center—it similarly draws your eye back to the beautiful art, and it looks nice and visually balanced, even as you remove pieces from the pool. Unfortunately, that's where the upsides of this design choice end. From a practical gameplay standpoint, it took me FAR too long to essentially discover accidentally that:
[olist][*]You can move the pieces inside the rings with the scroll wheel on your mouse; otherwise, you have to attempt to find spots in between the pieces (sometimes impossible) and drag to scroll through. What if you're playing on a trackpad or a mouse without a scroll wheel? Sucks to be you, I guess.
[*]Despite the fact that when you move the left inner (or outer) ring, the corresponding right inner (or outer) ring ALSO scrolls in the opposite direction, the pieces within the rings do NOT go all the way around, and in reality are four entirely unconnected pools of pieces. WHY does it work in this strangely misleading manner? I genuinely have no idea on this one, but there is no way to turn this feature off, if you'd like to keep at hand a piece in the right inner ring but scroll through the left inner ring, for example. I've looked, and as far as I can tell, it's impossible, that's simply baked into the game design. Which is, again...a choice, certainly.[/olist]

So... did I like [i]anything[/i] about this game? Well, I've mentioned it already, but the actual stained glass art is genuinely lovely; it's just about the only thing this game has going for it that I have no complaints about. The music is also very nice and did add to the experience for me at the beginning, but I must add the caveat that the loop is far too short for a game meant to be played for multiple hours; it gets repetitive fairly quickly, and I muted it entirely after about the first 40-50 minutes of gameplay. There is only the one song, and it does not change as you move from country to country or continent to continent.

Overall, I would love to support the artist who made the stained glass art used in this game, but I will not be buying any further titles from this company. I purchased this with a coupon for $1.84, and regrettably, that still borders on overpaying for the high level of design incompetence on display here; after sinking nearly four hours into it out of sheer completion stubbornness, I'd kind of rather have spent that on a bottle of soda. If you can get it for free, I'd say it's probably worth seeing if you can overlook the design flaws, as—based on the other reviews—some other people clearly can. Otherwise, skip buying this one and just go look up a YouTube video of the pretty art.

This was my hidden gem of the 2017 Summer Sale. It gave me that Pandora's Box vibe that I've longed to feel, since that old puzzle game had a charm of relaxing discovery that no game has come close to recreating, to say nothing about surpassing it. I wish someone would make a spiritual successor already...

Still, my double thumbs-up comes with a few caveats (don't let them dissuade you from playing the game!).

First of all, the art style can sometimes be detrimental to the game. There are rare times when the sheen and colour composition can make it difficult to discern which spaces are empty and which are not. It's not bad, more like a little too much of a good thing, maybe.

Secondly, the clock-like play area wasn't such a hot idea in retrospect. Each puzzle has you place stained glass fragments within a given clock-like object - a novel idea, but it feels a bit forced and constraining. It doesn't really add anything to the game other than making the play area even more visually busy than it already is.

Finally, the puzzle mechanics don't seem to lend themselves to increased scope. I realize the puzzles were intended to be solved blind with a small number of pieces, but I imagine solving anything with more pieces could be an exercise in frustration. These stained glass puzzles lend themselves to unorthodox pieces composition, so there is some potential there for unique puzzle-solving experiences.

Despite all of the above nitpicks, I wholeheartedly recommend the game to any puzzle afficionado in search of something relaxing and a little off the beaten path. I'm looking forward to what the devs cook up next.

I'm a bit of a perfectionist with my puzzling, so having pieces that didn't fit right - not the right size, extra protrusions on it, not exactly the right shape - was causing me untold grief in getting puzzles completed.  I'd hover a piece over a spot, say it didn't fit, drop the piece to have it magically slot into place with the clinking of glass fragments signaling it took...and still shaking my head saying the piece didn't fit there.

After those epiphanies puzzle completion sped up noticeably.  And after finishing the game I find myself really wanting to buy a stained glass clock.

So this review actually started out positive, but in writing it I realised that actually, as much as I want to, I don't think i can give it a positive review [i]as a game[/i].

Glass masquerade is a jigsaw-puzzle game, where you build up a stained glass window out of its pieces.

So first of all, this game is [i]gorgeous[/i]. Seriously, the art is fabulous, an each stage has a completely different design, and they are quite well themed to the chosen countries. The menus and the rest of the UI also have a nice scheme which fits with the overall theme and complements its well. There is some good design here.
The game is also very relaxing; its not especially difficult, and there is no time pressure, or any way to lose progress or otherwise fail, which for winding down in the evening is a big plus.

Unfortunately, the actual gameplay mechanics missed the mark in my opinion.
The shapes appear to the side, but they are masked - you only see the outline, and it is randomly rotated.
When you pick it to put into place it will spin to its correct orientation and highlight (returning to masked if you drop it), however, the highlight makes the colours look different, which until you work it out can be very confusing! It also makes the issue of sometimes the contrast with the background doesnt really work and its hard to tell which bits are what.
Added to this is the fact that the shapes snap in and shrink very slightly, and don't always [i]completely[/i] match the space they drop to and some of the more difficult puzzles become frustrating, which clashes horribly with the rest of the relaxing pace (which makes this even worse!). Oh and on some levels its hard to tell what the actual gameplay area is, just another compounding problem.

I have no problem with a game not having deep mechanics, and I really wanted to give it a positive review, but a game is a game, and therefore gameplay is king. And this one just didnt quite have that.
I'd probably recommend picking it up on sale.

[h1]10/10[/h1]

[b]Overall[/b]
I was surprised just how addicted I got to playing this game! If you enjoy jigsaw puzzles, or are just looking for a game to turn your brain off for an hour or two this is perfect.

[b]Puzzles[/b]
Difficulties vary depending on the puzzle but none of them will have you scratching your head for too long. Something that took me a while to notice was that the circular sliders aren't actually connected to one another - you have four rather than two pools of pieces to draw from, so if you feel stuck try scrolling through each one in turn.

[b]Achievements[/b]
Very easy to 100% this game as you will get an achievement for each puzzle you  complete. There's no requirement to buy paid DLC to complete the achievements; there is a free puzzle available for each DLC pack which will give you the "taster"  achievement for each one.

Glass Masquerade is a wonderful puzzle game with a focus on reconstructing watches faces with a wide variety of Art Deco and stained glass inspired imagery. Each watch piece is selected with from around the world in this "International Times Exhibition" along with more holiday (Halloween and Lunar New Year) as well as more abstract compositions found within the free and cheaply priced DLCs. 

Given this wide variety of compositions and puzzle piece shapes. this game gives you more than enough content for $4.99. The music, from what I can recall, is soothing and non-distracting, while the mechanics are enjoyable as you have to memorize the actual shape of the puzzle rather than the image. It's an interesting take on the classic puzzle. 

One note of complaint would have to be some of the "glitching" or a bug that can take place sometimes, where the puzzle piece can get stuck while moving/placing it down. In these brief moments the entire game will stop and get stuck, although I've found just hitting my menu button (the windows key). will help everything go back to normal. Personally, I didn't take much issue with this considering it was pretty infrequent, but I could see others taking issue with this. 

Overall, wonderful graphics and great puzzle comps. You'll likely find yourself purchasing the DLCs after finishing the main game, and even purchasing the second game as well.

This game was a massive disappointment.

It's not particularly hard, but there are things that feel arbitrarily "difficult", like the fact that the pieces are invisible and spin around when you grab them. Sure, this stops the game from being just a jigsaw game, but as it stands, it feels like they should be added difficulty parameters instead of the base thing.

The pieces look too big to fit in the holes until you try, and the fact that the pieces are located in dials that spin, hiding some of the pieces, feel like more busywork to deal with than actual puzzle difficulty.

The art is gorgeous, true, but at points noisy and a bit messy (that USA clock is horrible, sorry. No, I'm not from the US). The music is really nice, but at a 2 minute loop, it starts getting tiresome fast, even more noticeably so when there's a couple of seconds of silence between repetitions.

In the end, it's a game that was clearly made with love, but the end result is a game that leans too heavily in its aesthetics to be a competent puzzle game, and muddles the proceedings with unnecesary, arbitrary interface decisions that elevate difficulty artificially. 

Feels like making a jigsaw puzzle where you can't see which pieces you are picking up, and you can only grab one at a time. More aggravating than difficult.

We all have one of those games that we turn to to help us unwind and relax after a stressful day. 

In my case, it's not Glass Masquerade, but gods damn, if it ain't beautiful as hell. The music is lovely, and the puzzles are fairly challenging at times, all while providing some gorgeous stained glass designs as a form of reward for completing them.

There are, sadly, a couple of gripes, but they're pretty small ones.

The first is the issue with empty spaces not being the size of the pieces you'll be handling. More often than not, you'll be spending extra time trying to figure out where a shard will go, and wind up glancing over the exact spot time and time again, simply because the space is much smaller than the actual piece. 

The second gripe is that some puzzles have outer pieces, but the frames don't immediately tell you this. This means that you may spend several minutes trying to find a space for one shard, only to realize close to the end that it doesn't even go in the main design.

Really, it's not a bad game at all, and this is coing from someone who isn't a huge fan of puzzle games.
